A robot begins to tinker with its own mind while a scientist races to stop it. Two weeks ago, Dean W. Ball expressed concern on Hyperdimensional that the recursive self-improvement (RSI) conversation has become “unfocused, extreme, and dramatically oversimplified”. He reminded us that using a technology to build a better version of itself is as old as invention (e.g., humans using iron tools to make better iron tools; he calls this “weak recursion”). He expanded to say that the genuinely unprecedented risk is a technology like AI autonomously developing its own successor (e.g., AI autonomously building better AI; he calls this “strong recursion”). To avert strong recursion, he proposes greater transparency from frontier AI companies, based (in part) on metrics like how compute allocation decisions are made and “the share of merged code changes with no substantive human review”, which he suggests “could form the basis for a statutory definition” of strong recursion, giving policymakers a foundation for corporate liability. I’m persuaded by his argument, and below I take him up on his call for additional metrics. Accepting the two metric classes he proposes, I’ll focus my attention on the next problem: these two metrics are necessary but not sufficient for measuring strong recursion. First and foremost, neither compute allocation nor human intervention measures whether an AI training algorithm improved (e.g., less human intervention != stronger model). Secondly, neither metric establishes a hard link between human intervention and AI improvement (e.g., code changes != code improvement). Finally, neither overcomes a critical safety challenge: detecting strong recursion before we train each successively more capable model. In this post, I propose two metrics that address these challenges: sample complexity , which detects the mechanism of strong recursion without building a more capable AI, and counterfactual measurement , which measures how much AI capability changes when advise by AI tools. Ball’s argument for strong recursion rests on five steps, which I’ll restate here in order to pinpoint where strong recursion can be measured: R1: AI models perform AI research autonomously. R2: As a result of R1, AI algorithms improve faster. R3: As a result of R2, AI models get smarter faster. R4: As a result of R3, AI models get better at AI research (R1). R5: As a result of R1-R4, algorithmic improvements need no new infrastructure (just software updates) and so this loop can run very fast. With these steps established, let’s consider the measurability of R4 down to R1: R4: Is it better at AI research than its predecessor? This is measurable with existing evaluations. R3: Did its capabilities grow faster than the previous generation’s? This is also measurable, by comparing successive generations. R2: Did the training algorithm itself improve? This needs a measure that separates algorithmic progress from simply using better data or more compute. R1: Did the improvement happen without consequential human input? This needs a measure that distinguishes human involvement that mattered from involvement that was only a formality. R4 and R3 are measurable using existing evaluations. However, R2 and R1 require more advanced techniques: sample complexity and attribution. A researcher measures a robot which is less powerful than the full sized version Measuring Algorithmic Improvement Without Training A Smarter Model While pundits and policymakers often use AI benchmarks as evidence that AI algorithms are improving, increases in AI capability are merely circumstantial evidence for algorithmic progress. A model can become more capable for other reasons, such as training with better data or more compute; a benchmark score is too reductive to tell the difference. On the contrary, an AI algorithm can get worse while the model it trains gets smarter. As the Bitter Lesson opines, often the best way to build a smarter model is to dumb down the algorithm. Much of the decade’s progress on AI came from deliberately simpler, more data-hungry algorithms that scale better on more GPUs (e.g. this is the reason why the Transformer replaced LSTMs, as the authors describe ). To isolate the impact of algorithmic improvements on benchmark scores, we must disentangle two concepts: sample complexity and scaling laws. Sample Complexity. The central measure of algorithmic progress is sample complexity. For LLMs, sample complexity is the number of pre/post-training tokens needed to reach a pre-defined level of accuracy on a benchmark. The fewer tokens you needed, the better your algorithm learns, and the smarter your full-scale AI will be. Scaling Laws. Since about GPT-1, the central driver of capability growth in LLMs has been the scaling laws. Training on more tokens, stored in larger models using more compute, leads to higher accuracy on benchmarks. Unlike sample complexity, the more tokens you use, the better your model. The easiest way to disentangle the two is to treat sample complexity as a divisor on the scaling laws. With 2x the compute but 2x the sample complexity, you get 2x/2x = 1x, the same capability. With 2x the compute and 0.5x the sample complexity, it’s like having 4x the compute. With 1x the compute and 0.0001x the sample complexity, it’s like having 10,000x the compute. This makes sample complexity the right measure for R2, and it has an advantage that matters even more for governance: measuring sample complexity doesn’t require building a more capable model. Pick a fixed capability threshold below the frontier. With each new generation of methods, train to that threshold, record the tokens and compute it took (including inference compute), and stop. If the resources needed to reach the threshold start falling much faster than their historical trend across successive generations, the engine of strong recursion is turning. And we can learn that without ever producing a more capable model: verification without escalation. However, what sample complexity can’t tell us is who turned the engine. A faster-falling curve could reflect brilliant human researchers as easily as an autonomous AI. That’s the job of the second metric. A researcher (left) influences a robot with strings while a second researcher (right) studies their influence and writes down their observations. Robustly Measuring AI Impact on Algorithmic Research Productivity Measuring the impact of AI on strong recursion is about disentangling the impact of frontier AI researchers and AI agents on improvements to sample complexity. Let’s begin by looking at the typical workflow of AI researchers and agents: Research Steps (R1 - R8) A human observes a previous AI training run They develop an intuition as to why it didn’t learn faster. They iterate on that theory with AI agents They copy a recent training script into a new folder They use AI tools to edit that training script in a way which could test the theory They save that new training script into a company server (version controlled) They launch training runs on a small-ish amount of data (e.g., parameter sweep) They return to (1). Through this process, an AI researcher - sitting besides hundreds of other researchers - develops evidence that a particular approach improves either sample complexity (more intelligence per sample) or the ability to scale (can load more samples into the same GPU infrastructure in less time). And if researcher is successful, they submit their idea to the “big training run” team to include in the next major large-scale training run, and - if things go well - in the next major AI release. So where is the opportunity for AI acceleration? In the 8 research steps (R1-R8), an AI researcher benefits from AI tools during R3 and R5. And the data they most naturally collect is the speed of sample complexity improvements coming from AI researchers working with AI agents to develop new algorithms. However, to truly disentangle the role of AI agents we also need to measure the counterfactual: how much would sample complexity have improved without AI assistance on R3 and R5? For measuring impact on R5, the measurement can be taken - even after the fact. Any AI company could take the base training code and pay a second engineer to (without using AI tools) modify that code with the idea from the aformentioned AI researcher. If the modification took 3 hours with AI assistance and 90 minutes with AI assistance, then we know that AI is speeding up R5 by a factor of 2x. However, measuring the impact of AI agents on R3 is the most expensive part of the whole business. Given how non-linear the creative process is (would the researcher come to the same conclusions with/without AI?… hard to say), there’s only one way I can think of to measure it: frontier AI labs would need to set aside random subsets of their algorithmic research teams (e.g. perhaps 10%), to do algorithmic research without AI assistance. Taken together, if society deems it necessary for strong recursion to be measured, the following concrete steps could do so: Develop AI Research Benchmarks: these benchmarks should evaluate the degree to which an AI can take a training script and improve its sample complexity. Karpathy’s autoresearch already has the makings of one. Measure Sample Complexity During Small-Scale Research: For each small-scale experiment, frontier AI researchers calculate a sample complexity measurement w.r.t. an AI research-focused sample complexity benchmark. Every two weeks, a random 1%-10% of frontier AI researchers spend the next 2 weeks ideating and building without AI tools: They would come up with ideas and implement them in code without the assistance that AI provides, also calculating sample complexity measurements. A combination of (1) and (2) provide grounded measurements of strong recursion: at a mild cost to frontier AI research capacity, AI labs provide grounded RSI metrics upon which a wider set of safety programs can operate. This would be quite expensive for the labs, and I imagine AI researchers would have mixed reviews on attempting to make progress the old-school way. Weak recursion is just the scaling laws. These are trivial to measure by running multiple training runs using today’s AI algorithms but various data checkpoints over time. You can see one such example in Dwarkesh’s post on pretraining progress . Impact of AI algorithms vs data A Less Expensive Way to Measure Ball’s “strong recursion” However, given that weak recursion is so inexpensive to run (periodically re-run frontier AI algorithms against old data), then it opens up a way to indirectly measure strong recursion. If we how much more accurate an AI system has gotten (culmination of both strong and weak recursion), and we can disentangle how much of that improvement came from data and scale (weak recursion), then we know the sum total of strong recursion indirectly. And given that strong recursion is a function of two factors (AI helping ideation + AI assisted coding), and we can staff-out the AI assisted coding to dedicated engineering teams (have them re-implement coding changes without AI help), it seems that we can even back into realistic estimates for how much AI is helping with research ideation. To evaluate whether this inexpensive, indirect measure of strong recursion is (or could be made) accurate, I would like to recommend that frontier AI labs conduct a 1-time experiment: set aside 10% of their frontier AI research teams to do their ideation without AI assistance for 1 month, and then use that ground-truth data to calibrate the degree to which this indirect method of measuring strong recursion is accurate. If it holds well, then in theory all frontier AI labs could report metrics of both strong and weak recursion, grounding the potential for governance regimes such as the liability regime suggested by Ball in his piece.
